fix(desktop): resolve POSIX-style Windows asset paths

HTML Apps use forward-slash asset URLs as their base, and workspace
file paths flow through the renderer as POSIX-style strings. On Windows
these arrive at the main process as "/C:/notes/..." with a leading
slash before the drive letter. path.resolve treats that as
drive-relative and prepends the current drive ("C:\C:\notes\..."),
which fails the granted-scope check, so the hubble-asset:// protocol
served nothing: HTML Apps rendered blank and local images 404'd.

Normalize the leading slash before a drive letter in resolvePath so
these paths resolve to a real Windows path. macOS/Linux are unaffected
(guarded on process.platform === "win32").

fix(desktop): send forward-slash paths to the renderer on Windows

The renderer builds paths with forward slashes, but the main process
returned native paths (backslash on Windows) from the directory
listing, launch workspace path, folder/file pickers, watch events, and
open-file events. The mix broke the sidebar's path helpers: relative-
path stripping failed, so the workspace root and folders became phantom
nested nodes (C: > Scratch > ...) and folder ids fed back into absolute-
path joins produced doubled paths like "C:\ws/C:/ws/new-file.md" —
breaking New file, New folder, and Reveal in File Explorer, and showing
the workspace twice in the sidebar.

Add toRendererPath() and apply it at every main->renderer path boundary
so the renderer always sees forward slashes (collectWorkspaceFiles and
the image-paste path already did this). resolvePath already normalizes
them coming back. macOS/Linux are unaffected (path.sep is already "/").

Prototype a command mode for the global palette

Adds command mode to the existing GlobalSearchPalette. Cmd+P keeps today's
file search unchanged; typing "/" at the start of the query switches to
running commands, and deleting it switches back. One dialog, one keybinding,
no mode to remember.

Every command surfaced here already works in Hubble today. The palette is a
discoverability layer, not new capability -- several commands (Reveal in File
Manager, Copy File Path, Chat About This Note, Toggle Sidebar) previously had
no menu entry at all and were reachable only by knowing their shortcut.

Commands project over the command registry: label, default binding, and
enablement all come from `getCommand(id)`, so the palette cannot disagree with
the menu bar or the key handler about what a command is called, what it is
bound to, or when it applies. Only the palette's own concerns -- grouping,
search synonyms, and the handler -- are declared locally, alongside the few
actions that have no registry entry (new folder, theme, zoom, updates).

Reading labels from the registry also fixes an inversion: app.open-folder is
the workspace switcher and app.add-folder opens a folder into the sidebar,
which an independent set of labels had backwards.

Disabled commands are dropped from the list rather than shown greyed out, so
no result can be selected but not run. Ranking reuses the existing fuzzy
scorer -- labels at full weight, keywords and group names discounted -- with
recency only breaking ties, so a learned ordering never outranks a stronger
text match.

Editor commands need an editor instance the palette does not have, so
EditorView registers the mounted editor in a single-slot module. Its list
actions call Hubble's own toggleParentBulletList/OrderedList/TaskList rather
than TipTap's, which silently no-op here because Hubble models a task list as
a bullet list of task items.

Zoom gains a renderer IPC so the palette can dispatch it; the accelerators
stay owned by the View menu.

Show the command prefix as a chip, not a character

Typing "/" now promotes the prefix out of the query text into a chip in the
input's leading slot, and Backspace on an empty command query removes it. The
query itself only ever holds search terms, so the prefix is a state the input
is in rather than a character to read past and edit around.

Drops the terminal icon with it. A terminal glyph framed the palette as a
code-editor feature; the chip is the prefix itself, which is both friendlier
and more literal about how you got here.

Mode moves from derived to held state, since the query no longer carries the
prefix that used to encode it.

Add hubble.links.open so HTML Apps can open external links

HTML Apps render in a sandboxed iframe without allow-popups or
allow-top-navigation, so window.open and target="_blank" are no-ops
and apps have no way to send the user to an external URL.

Add a links.open method to the runtime broker: the injected runtime
exposes hubble.links.open(url) / hubble.links.safeOpen(url) in the
same style as files.*, and the renderer dispatch validates the URL
(http/https only, mirroring the main-process guard) before forwarding
to the existing desktop:open-external-url IPC handler. No new IPC
surface is added.

Closes #262

Open plain http(s) anchor clicks externally from HTML Apps

The runtime routes anchor clicks on absolute http(s) links through the
same links.open broker request the hubble.links API uses, so authored
HTML works without calling the API. Relative and in-page links resolve
to hubble-asset:// and are untouched; app click handlers can call
preventDefault to opt out.

Show the desktop window before the renderer loads

The window stayed hidden until `did-finish-load`, so launching the app
meant a bouncing dock icon and nothing else for the whole renderer boot.
Show it right after the full-screen/maximize restore instead: the window
opens as a correctly themed, correctly scaled frame that content fills in.

That is only safe once nothing the show path used to wait on happens after
load, so the three settings move ahead of the window:

- zoom is passed as `webPreferences.zoomFactor`, which Chromium applies
  itself instead of a `setZoomFactor` call after load
- the traffic-light inset is passed as a launch argument and written by
  preload with `webFrame.insertCSS` at document start, replacing an awaited
  `executeJavaScript` round-trip
- the background color is set on the BrowserWindow and mirrored by an inline
  `<style>` in index.html, so the native frame, the boot canvas and the
  mounted app are all `--background` and there is no flash

`ready-to-show` looks like the right hook but is not: with a body of just
`<div id="root">` there is nothing to paint until React mounts, so it fired
0.1-0.2 ms before `did-finish-load` in every measured run.

Also minify all three build targets (electron-vite defaults them to
`minify: false`) and move `shadcn` to devDependencies, where a build-time
CLI belongs.

Window visible drops from 370 ms to 165 ms after `main.js` starts, median
of 5 warm runs. The renderer chunk halves to 2,467 KB and app.asar drops
from 131 MB to 56 MB.

Closes #279

Add tabs to the desktop editor (#240)

Several notes can be open at once as tabs, with one visible at a time.
Each tab keeps its own back/forward trail and its own scroll position.

A tab records where a note is, not what it holds: its path and its
trail. The open document stays singular — one file loaded, one editor,
one watcher — and activating a tab saves the current note and loads the
tab's note, which is what clicking a sidebar row already did. Per-tab
document buffers were considered and rejected: the single-document
assumption is load-bearing in reads, not only writes, so savePathContent,
the auto-title liveness check, and updateMovedLinks would all quietly
come to mean "the focused document" while still compiling.

Opening a note explicitly, from the sidebar or the palette, gives it a
tab or focuses the one already showing it. Following a link stays in the
current tab, which is what its trail is for.

Leaving a note now goes through one place that saves it, records where
the user was, and refuses when the file has changed on disk. That also
fixes a standing bug: typing without pausing and immediately opening
another note dropped the last edit, because the editor's unmount flush
ran after the store had moved on.

Tabs are session state and are not persisted, so relaunch restores the
last opened note as a single tab.

fix(desktop): raise the window when macOS opens a file into a running app

macOS delivers a document to an already-running app through `open-file`, not
`second-instance`, and that handler only forwarded the path to the renderer.
The file loaded but the window stayed behind whatever app was in front, and
with no window open (⌘W on macOS keeps the app alive) the IPC was dropped by
`sendToRenderer`'s optional chain, so nothing happened at all.

Both handlers now share `revealForOpenFile`, which restores and raises the
window, or creates one when the app is running without any.

Fixes #287

fix(desktop): share one window-creation lock across every caller

Review catch: `app.isReady()` is true well before the bootstrap finishes, so an
`open-file` or `second-instance` arriving during it could start a second
`createWindow()` while the first was still awaiting `loadWindowState()`.

`ensureMainWindow()` now holds the in-flight promise, and `whenReady`,
`activate`, and the open-file path all go through it. The open-file path waits
for `appBootstrapped` as well, so a window it creates always has the IPC
handlers its renderer calls during init.
